analysis.one_liner: Charges opioid makers a per-milligram fee to fund addiction treatment programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a one-cent-per-milligram fee on opioid painkillers at the point of manufacture or import, with the money going to states to fund substance abuse treatment: new treatment facilities, longer residential programs, housing for people in recovery, and recruitment of addiction specialists in rural and underserved areas. Cancer and hospice patients would be rebated or discounted so they pay none of the fee, and the Health and Human Services Department would have to report to Congress on how the fee affected drug prices and patient access.
analysis.who_benefits: People with opioid addiction and their communities would gain access to more treatment programs, residential care, recovery housing, and providers in underserved areas, all funded by the fee. Cancer and hospice patients who need opioids for pain would pay nothing out of pocket because of the rebate program.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-cent-per-milligram fee on opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers, and excludes addiction-treatment medications like those used in medically assisted treatment from the fee.

Requires any net revenue after patient rebates to flow to states under the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant program, to be used exclusively for substance abuse efforts, including new treatment facilities, sober living homes, long-term residential programs, housing for children of parents in treatment, and care for babies born with neonatal abstinence syndrome.
Requires states to use part of the funding to recruit, train, and increase reimbursement for substance use disorder professionals in rural and medically underserved communities.
Requires HHS to rebate or discount the fee for cancer and hospice patients so they face no economic burden, and to report to Congress on the fee's impact on opioid prices and patient access.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers, producers, and importers would pay the fee. They could pass some of it through to the price of opioid painkillers, which is why the bill builds in rebates for cancer and hospice patients and a two-year study of the fee's effect on retail prices.

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise the cost of opioid pain relievers, and patients outside the cancer and hospice carve-out, such as some chronic pain patients, could face higher drug prices if manufacturers pass the fee through.
A per-milligram excise is a blunt instrument: its revenue depends on how many opioids are sold, so funding for treatment would rise and fall with opioid sales volumes rather than with treatment need.
The bill leaves the size of the treatment expansion entirely dependent on fee collections after rebates; if opioid sales fell sharply, states would get correspondingly less money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed to place the cost of the opioid epidemic's treatment gap on the manufacturers of the products involved, while protecting the patients most dependent on opioids for legitimate pain from paying the fee. Its main design weakness is that funding for treatment is tied to opioid sales volumes, and some non-exempt patients could still see higher prices. The core tradeoff is small and targeted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 115th Congress.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers are better off because the bill never advanced: they never had to pay the one-cent-per-milligram fee on their sales, and no new dedicated funding stream for state addiction treatment was created.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing the opioid stewardship fee and treatment block grants.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and its Health Subcommittee for the entire Congress without a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of additional referral (jurisdiction over the excise tax provision)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by sequential referral and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and no Republican action is recorded on it.

industries.note: The bill would charge them one cent per milligram on every active opioid they sell, a direct cost on their core product. They benefit from the bill's failure because they never paid the fee.

The bill would direct new funding to treatment facilities, residential programs, recovery housing, and provider recruitment, creating demand for treatment services. The bill died, so no new funding arrived.
